intro: A warrior sits down in his chariot and refuses to fight. His charioteer answers him in about 700 verses. That conversation, the Bhagavad Gita, is one of the most read and most translated books in the world. Many Hindus recite it daily, read it at funerals, and turn to it in hard moments.

In this unit you will read Gita chapters 1 to 6 closely. You will follow Arjuna's grief, Krishna's first answers about the self, the steady mind, and the discipline of action. You will compare Telang's prose translation (1882) with Arnold's verse (1885), and meet readers such as Gandhi and Tilak who drew very different lessons from the same verses.

By the end you will be able to cite a Gita verse by chapter and number, explain what it says and who is speaking, and describe how different readers have understood it, without deciding for anyone which reading is true.
bigQuestion: What does the Gita teach about action and duty, and why do its readers disagree about what that means?

title: Close Reading the Bhagavad Gita

chapters.title: Arjuna's Despair and Krishna's Answer
chapters.bigQuestion: What does Krishna say to a person who cannot bring himself to act, and how have readers understood his answer?

story.title: The Bow Falls
story.kicker: In the middle of two armies, the greatest archer of his age sits down and refuses to fight.
paragraphs: Two armies face each other on the plain of Kurukshetra. Conch shells blow. Horses stamp. The Bhagavad Gita opens here, inside the Mahabharata, at the last moment before a great war between cousins. The blind king Dhritarashtra asks his minister Sanjaya what is happening, and Sanjaya describes it.

Arjuna, the finest archer among the Pandava brothers, asks his charioteer to drive into the open space between the lines. His charioteer is Krishna. Arjuna wants to see who he must fight. He looks across and sees his teachers, his great-uncle Bhishma, his cousins, and the sons of friends.

His limbs go weak. His mouth goes dry. His bow, Gandiva, slips from his hand. He says he does not want victory or a kingdom if it costs the lives of his own family. What good would a throne be, he asks, if the people he loves are dead?

At the end of the first chapter, Arjuna sits down in the chariot, overcome with grief. In the second chapter he says plainly that he will not fight. Then he asks Krishna to teach him what is right. The other seventeen chapters of the Gita are Krishna's answer.

Hindus have read this scene for more than two thousand years. Some see a real warrior on a real field. Others see every person who stands frozen before a hard duty. In this chapter you will read Gita 1 and 2 closely and meet both kinds of reader.
story.think: Arjuna refuses to act because he loves his family. Is his refusal weakness, wisdom, or something else? What would you need to know to decide?

lessons.title: A Poem Inside an Epic
lessons.mainIdea: The Gita is eighteen chapters of the Mahabharata's Bhishma Parva, told by Sanjaya to a blind king.
reading: The Bhagavad Gita, or "Song of the Lord," is not a separate book in its origin. It sits inside the *Mahabharata*, the great Sanskrit epic, in the section called the Bhishma Parva. It has 18 chapters and about 700 verses. Most of the verses are in a meter called shloka.

The Gita has layers of speakers. The blind king Dhritarashtra asks a question in verse 1.1. His minister Sanjaya, who has been given special sight, reports what he sees on the field. Inside Sanjaya's report, Arjuna speaks and Krishna answers. So the whole *dialogue* reaches us through a narrator.

Scholars usually date the Gita to about the 2nd century BCE to the 2nd century CE, while noting it is hard to be exact. Hindu tradition places the war at the start of the Kali Yuga, often dated 3102 BCE, and names the sage Vyasa as the author of the epic. Both dates are worth knowing, because readers use them for different purposes.

words.d: the long Sanskrit epic of the war between the Pandava and Kaurava cousins; the Gita is part of it
a text built from speakers asking and answering; the Gita is a dialogue between Arjuna and Krishna
the sixth book of the Mahabharata, where the Gita appears

check.q: Who narrates the events on the battlefield to King Dhritarashtra?
check.why: In Gita 1.1 the blind king asks, and his minister Sanjaya reports what he sees.

check.q: Where is the Gita found?

In the Bhishma Parva of the Mahabharata
check.why: The Gita is part of the Mahabharata's Bhishma Parva, not the Ramayana or the Vedas.

lessons.title: Who Stands on the Field
lessons.mainIdea: Arjuna's crisis begins when he sees that the enemy is his own family and teachers.
reading: In Gita 1.21 to 1.23, Arjuna asks Krishna to place the chariot between the two armies. Krishna is his friend, cousin and charioteer. Arjuna wants to look at the men who have come to fight for the Kauravas, the sons of Dhritarashtra. The Kaurava army is led by Duryodhana, the eldest of those sons.

What he sees, in verses 1.26 to 1.27, is a list of relatives. There are fathers and grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons and friends. Bhishma raised him. Drona taught him archery. The war is a *kinship* war, and that is the heart of his pain.

The Mahabharata tells how the war came about: a stolen kingdom, a rigged dice game, years of exile and failed peace talks. Arjuna's side believes it has a just claim. Yet the Gita shows him feeling that even a just war is unbearable when it is fought against those you love.

words.d: the five sons of Pandu, including Yudhishthira and Arjuna
the sons of Dhritarashtra, led by Duryodhana, cousins of the Pandavas
family ties; Arjuna's enemies are his kin

look.title: A List of Faces
look.text: In Gita 1.26 Arjuna sees, standing in both armies, fathers, grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons and companions. The poem gives a list, not a crowd.
look.prompt: Why might the poet list family roles instead of saying "the enemy army"? What does the list make a reader feel?

check.q: Why does Arjuna ask Krishna to drive between the armies?
choices: To see who he must fight
check.why: In Gita 1.21–1.23 Arjuna wants to look at those who have come to fight.

check.q: Who are the Kauravas?
choices: The sons of Dhritarashtra, cousins of the Pandavas
check.why: The Kauravas are Dhritarashtra's sons; the Pandavas are Pandu's sons.

check.q: What makes this war especially painful for Arjuna?
choices: He must fight his relatives and teachers
check.why: Gita 1.26–1.27 lists the family and teachers on the other side.

lessons.title: Arjuna's Arguments
lessons.mainIdea: Arjuna gives reasons for refusing: killing kin is wrong, and it will destroy families and their traditions.
reading: Arjuna does not only feel sad. He argues. In Gita 1.31 to 1.46 he says he wants no victory or pleasure if it comes from killing kin. He says even if his enemies are greedy, he should not become like them. He also says that killing them would bring sin on his own side, not only on theirs.

He then warns about the wider damage. When families are destroyed, he says, their family *dharma* is lost. Dharma here means duty and right order, the ways a family keeps its rites and its care for the dead. Arjuna fears that disorder will spread when the elders are gone.

Close readers notice something. Arjuna uses the language of dharma to argue against fighting. Krishna will later use the language of dharma to argue for it. The Gita stages a real argument about what duty requires, and it lets Arjuna's case be heard in full before any answer comes.

words.d: duty, right order, the right way to live; the Gita debates what it requires
reasons given for a position; Arjuna argues against fighting
family dharma: the duties and rites that keep a family's traditions alive

look.title: Arjuna Refuses
look.text: Arjuna says he does not wish to kill his teachers and kin even if they would kill him, not even for rule over the three worlds, much less for the earth. What joy could come from killing Dhritarashtra's sons?
look.cite: Bhagavad Gita 1.35–1.36, paraphrased from K.T. Telang's translation (SBE 8, 1882)
look.prompt: What is Arjuna weighing against what? Put his reasoning into one sentence of your own.

check.q: What does Arjuna fear will happen when families are destroyed?
choices: The Pandavas will lose their kingdom forever
Family dharma and traditions will be lost
The Vedas will be forgotten by the gods
check.why: In Gita 1.40 onward Arjuna argues that family dharma perishes when families are destroyed.

check.q: What is notable about the way Arjuna argues?
choices: He refuses to give any reasons
He argues that the gods do not exist
He uses the idea of dharma to argue against fighting
check.why: Arjuna and Krishna both appeal to dharma, which makes the Gita a real debate.

check.q: In Gita 1.35, what would Arjuna refuse even for rule over the three worlds?
check.why: He says he would not kill them even for the three worlds, much less for the earth.

lessons.title: Krishna's First Reply
lessons.mainIdea: Krishna begins by telling Arjuna that the wise do not grieve for the living or the dead.
reading: In Gita 2.1 to 2.10, Arjuna says he is confused about his duty. He asks Krishna to teach him, calling himself Krishna's student. This is a turning point. The friend in the chariot now becomes a *guru*, a teacher. In Hindu tradition a guru is honored as the one who removes the darkness of not knowing.

Krishna's first words surprise many readers. In 2.11 he says Arjuna grieves for those who should not be grieved for, yet speaks words that sound wise. The wise, he says, grieve neither for the living nor for the dead. It is a gentle rebuke: Krishna says Arjuna's words sound wise, but his grief is misplaced.

Krishna then begins to explain why. His first argument is about the self, called *atman* in later teaching and dehin, "the embodied one," in these verses. The Gita says this self was never born and never dies. The rest of chapter 2 builds on that claim.

words.d: a teacher, especially of spiritual knowledge; Arjuna asks Krishna to teach him
the self; in the Gita, the self that is said not to be born or to die
"the embodied one"; the Gita's word for the self living in a body

look.title: Student and Teacher
look.text: In Gita 2.7 Arjuna says his nature is overcome by weakness and his mind is confused about duty. He asks what is truly better, and says, I am your disciple; teach me, for I come to you for refuge.
look.prompt: Why might the Gita have Arjuna ask to be taught before Krishna begins? How does that change the kind of talk that follows?

check.q: What happens in Gita 2.7?
choices: Arjuna asks Krishna to teach him as a disciple
Arjuna picks up his bow and fights
check.why: In 2.7 Arjuna becomes a student and asks for teaching; the universal form comes in chapter 11.

check.q: What does Krishna say about grief in Gita 2.11?
choices: Grief is the highest form of devotion
The wise grieve neither for the living nor for the dead
check.why: Krishna's first teaching is that the wise do not grieve for the living or the dead.

check.q: What does "dehin" mean in Gita 2?
choices: The embodied one, the self in a body
check.why: Dehin names the self that lives in a body.

lessons.title: Never Born, Never Dying
lessons.mainIdea: In Gita 2.19 to 2.21 Krishna says the self neither kills nor is killed, because it is unborn and eternal.
reading: Gita 2.19 says that anyone who thinks the self kills, or thinks it is killed, does not understand. The self does not kill and is not killed. Verse 2.20 adds that it is not born and does not die. It is unborn, everlasting and ancient, and it is not slain when the body is slain.

These verses are among the most quoted in the Gita. Many Hindus recite them at funerals and in times of loss. Readers find comfort in them because they describe death as the end of a body, not of the person's deepest self. Families may hear the verses in Sanskrit, in Hindi or Tamil, or in English, depending on where they live.

Some readers also notice a hard edge. Krishna uses this teaching to answer a man who does not want to kill. Critics, including some modern Hindu thinkers, ask whether the teaching could excuse violence. Defenders reply that the Gita is teaching about the self, not giving a license to harm. You will meet this debate again.

words.d: without beginning or end; the Gita calls the self eternal
never coming into being; Gita 2.20 says the self is unborn
reading sacred verses aloud at a funeral; Gita 2 is often read this way

look.title: Not Slain
look.text: The self is not born, nor does it ever die. Having once been, it will never again not be. It is unborn, everlasting, unchanging and primeval; it is not killed when the body is killed.
look.cite: Bhagavad Gita 2.20, paraphrased from K.T. Telang's translation (SBE 8, 1882)
look.prompt: Find the words in this verse that deny time (born, die, again). Why might this verse be read at funerals?

check.q: According to Gita 2.19, what does the self do?
choices: It neither kills nor is killed
It kills but is not killed
It is killed but reborn at once as a god
It lives only as long as the body
check.why: Gita 2.19 says the self does not kill and is not killed.

check.q: Why do many Hindus recite Gita 2.20 at times of loss?
choices: It describes death as the end of the body, not the deepest self
It names the dead person's next birth
It is the first verse of the Rig Veda
check.why: The verse says the self is not slain when the body is slain, which many mourners find comforting.

check.q: What worry have some critics raised about Gita 2.19–2.21?
choices: The verses are written in Tamil
The verses contradict the Ramayana's dates
The teaching might be used to excuse violence
The verses were added in 1885 by Arnold
check.why: Because Krishna uses the teaching to urge fighting, some readers ask if it could excuse harm; defenders answer that it is about the self.

lessons.title: The Clothing Image
lessons.mainIdea: Gita 2.22 compares the self changing bodies to a person changing worn-out clothes.
reading: The Gita often teaches through pictures. In 2.22 Krishna says that as a person throws off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, so the embodied self throws off worn-out bodies and enters new ones. This is the *clothing image*. Students often find it the easiest verse in chapter 2 to remember.

The image carries the idea of *samsara*, the cycle of birth, death and rebirth. Hindus who hold this teaching believe the self passes through many lives. The body is like a garment: needed, worn for a time, then set aside. The person wearing it, the text says, is not the same as the garment.

Verses 2.23 and 2.24 add more pictures. Weapons do not cut the self, fire does not burn it, water does not wet it, wind does not dry it. The poet takes the four things that destroy bodies and says none of them reach the self. When you read closely, watch how the Gita moves from an argument to a picture that makes the argument easy to remember.

words.d: the cycle of birth, death and rebirth described in Hindu texts
Gita 2.22's comparison of changing bodies to changing clothes
a word picture that carries an idea; the Gita teaches through images

look.title: New Clothes
look.text: As a man, casting off old clothes, puts on others and new ones, so the embodied self, casting off old bodies, goes to others and new ones.
look.cite: Bhagavad Gita 2.22, paraphrased closely from K.T. Telang's translation (SBE 8, 1882)
look.prompt: What in the picture stays the same, and what changes? What does the image suggest about how Arjuna should see death?

check.q: In Gita 2.22, what are worn-out bodies compared to?
choices: A river flowing to the sea
check.why: The clothing image compares bodies to garments that are cast off and replaced.

check.q: Which idea does the clothing image carry?
check.why: The image describes the self moving to new bodies, the teaching of samsara.

check.q: What does Gita 2.23 say about the self?
choices: It can be burned but not cut
Weapons, fire, water and wind cannot harm it
It dies with the body but returns later
check.why: Verse 2.23 lists four things that harm bodies and says none reach the self.

lessons.title: Your Right Is to the Work
lessons.mainIdea: Gita 2.47 says a person's concern is the action itself, not its fruits.
reading: Gita 2.47 may be the single most quoted verse of the book. Krishna tells Arjuna that his right, or concern, is with action alone, never with its fruits. He should not let the fruits be his motive, and he should not cling to doing nothing either. Each clause is short, and each one closes a door that Arjuna might try to walk through.

The word *karma* here means action, the deeds a person does. The "fruits" are the results. The verse does not say results do not matter. It says a person should not let the hope of reward, or fear of loss, drive the action. Readers call this acting without attachment.

Verse 2.48 follows. It asks Arjuna to act while steady in *yoga*, letting go of attachment and staying the same in success and failure. It then gives a short definition: evenness of mind is called yoga. In the Gita, yoga is much more than exercise; it names a disciplined way of acting and seeing.

words.d: action; also the teaching that actions bring results in this or later lives
the results or rewards of what one does
in the Gita, a discipline or path; 2.48 calls evenness of mind yoga

look.title: Action, Not Fruit
look.text: Your business is with action alone; not by any means with fruit. Let not the fruit of action be your motive to action. Let not your attachment be fixed on inaction.
look.cite: Bhagavad Gita 2.47, K.T. Telang, The Bhagavadgita (Sacred Books of the East 8, 1882); Telang's bracketed words removed
look.prompt: Name one job, sport or school task where focusing on the work instead of the grade might change how you do it.

check.q: According to Gita 2.47, what is a person's concern?
check.why: Gita 2.47 says one's business is with action alone, not with its fruits.

check.q: What does Gita 2.48 call yoga?
check.why: Verse 2.48 defines yoga as evenness of mind in success and failure.

check.q: Does Gita 2.47 tell Arjuna to do nothing?
choices: No; it warns against attachment to inaction too
Yes; it says inaction is best
Yes; it tells him to leave the field
No; it tells him to seek rewards
check.why: The last line of 2.47 warns against clinging to inaction.

lessons.title: The Person of Steady Wisdom
lessons.mainIdea: In Gita 2.54 to 2.72 Arjuna asks what a person of steady wisdom is like, and Krishna describes one.
reading: In 2.54 Arjuna asks a practical question. How does a person of steady wisdom speak, sit and walk? The Sanskrit term is *sthitaprajna*, one whose wisdom stands firm. Arjuna wants a picture of a real person, not a theory. His question tells us the Gita cares about how wisdom looks in daily life.

Krishna answers in verses 2.55 to 2.72. Such a person gives up desires that race through the mind. They are not shaken by sorrow and do not crave pleasure. They are free from fear and anger. Verse 2.58 uses a tortoise that draws its limbs into its shell as a picture of drawing the senses back from their objects.

Gandhi said these closing verses of chapter 2 were the verses he returned to most. They were recited daily at his ashram prayers. For many readers, the sthitaprajna is a goal to work toward slowly, one habit at a time. Readers from many traditions have also found in these verses a portrait of calm under pressure.

words.d: a person of steady wisdom, described in Gita 2.55–2.72
sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch; the Gita pictures drawing them back like a tortoise's limbs
calm evenness of mind in good times and bad

look.title: The Tortoise
look.text: Gita 2.58: when a person draws the senses back from their objects on every side, as a tortoise draws in its limbs, that person's wisdom is steady.
look.prompt: What does a tortoise do when it is in danger? What might it mean for a person to "draw in" the senses, and when might that help?

check.q: What does sthitaprajna mean?
check.why: Sthitaprajna means one whose wisdom stands firm, described in Gita 2.55–2.72.

check.q: What animal does Gita 2.58 use as an image?
choices: A tortoise drawing in its limbs
check.why: The tortoise withdrawing its limbs pictures drawing the senses back.

check.q: Which modern leader said the end of Gita 2 was especially important to him?
check.why: Gandhi said he returned to these verses and had them recited at his ashram.

lessons.title: From Desire to Ruin
lessons.mainIdea: Gita 2.62 to 2.63 traces a chain from dwelling on things to desire, anger, confusion and ruin.
reading: Gita 2.62 and 2.63 form a famous chain. When a person dwells on the objects of the senses, attachment grows. From attachment comes desire. From desire comes anger. From anger comes confusion. From confusion, memory wanders; from that, understanding is lost; and from that, the person is ruined.

This is a *causal chain*: each step causes the next. The Gita uses it to show why steadiness matters. The point is not that feelings are bad. It is that an unchecked thought can grow step by step into something that harms a person. The chain moves inward first, into memory and understanding, before it ends in ruin.

Teachers of many backgrounds have compared this chain to ideas in psychology. Some Hindu teachers use it in talks on anger. When you study it, notice the poem's method: it names a small first step, then shows how far the path can go. That method, a short list with a clear direction, makes the teaching easy to recite and remember.

words.d: a series of steps where each causes the next
clinging to something or someone; the Gita warns against it
wanting; in Gita 2.62 desire grows out of attachment

look.title: Steps in Gita 2.62–2.63
look.prompt: At which step do you think it would be easiest to stop the chain? Give a reason.

check.q: In Gita 2.62, what comes directly from attachment?
check.why: The chain runs: dwelling, attachment, desire, anger, confusion, loss of memory and understanding, ruin.

check.q: What comes directly from desire in the chain?
check.why: Gita 2.62 says anger arises from desire.

check.q: What is the main purpose of the chain in Gita 2.62–2.63?
choices: To list the Pandava brothers in order
To give the rules of the dice game
To show how a small thought can grow into harm
check.why: The chain shows why steadiness matters by tracing where unchecked desire leads.

lessons.title: Arnold's Song Celestial
lessons.mainIdea: Edwin Arnold's 1885 verse translation brought the Gita to many English readers, including the young Gandhi.
reading: In 1885 the English poet Edwin Arnold published The Song Celestial, a translation of the Gita in English verse. He made it rhyme and flow like Victorian poetry. It became popular in Britain and the United States. By 1900 it had gone through many editions, and it remains in print today.

Gandhi wrote in his autobiography that he first read the Gita as a law student in London, in Arnold's version, when two friends invited him to read it with them. He had not read it in Sanskrit or Gujarati before. That encounter, he said, began his lifelong study of the book.

A verse *translation* like Arnold's is beautiful but free. It adds words to fit rhyme and meter. K.T. Telang's prose translation of 1882, in the Sacred Books of the East series, stays closer to the Sanskrit. Close readers compare both, and they always name which one they are quoting.

words.d: a text carried from one language into another; every translation makes choices
a translation written as poetry, often freer than prose
a 50-volume series of English translations edited by F. Max Müller (1879–1910)

look.title: Two Kinds of Translation
look.text: Telang (1882) is prose that follows the Sanskrit closely and puts added words in brackets. Arnold (1885) is rhymed English verse that adds images to fit the meter. Both render Gita 2.47.
look.prompt: If you were writing a close-reading essay, which would you quote to show exactly what the Sanskrit says? Which might you quote to show how the Gita was felt by English readers?

check.q: What is The Song Celestial?
choices: Edwin Arnold's 1885 verse translation of the Gita
check.why: The Song Celestial is Arnold's English verse Gita of 1885.

check.q: Where did Gandhi first read the Gita, by his own account?
choices: In Sanskrit at school in Gujarat
In prison in Pune, in Marathi
check.why: Gandhi's autobiography says he first read it as a law student in London in Arnold's version.

check.q: Why do close readers often prefer Telang's prose for exact wording?
choices: It follows the Sanskrit more closely
It was written first in English by Krishna
check.why: Telang's prose stays near the Sanskrit; Arnold's verse is freer.

lessons.title: An Outer War or an Inner One
lessons.mainIdea: Some readers take Kurukshetra as a real battle; others read it as the struggle inside every person.
reading: Many Hindus read the Gita as a record of real events. On this *literal reading*, Arjuna was a real warrior, the war was real, and Krishna taught him on the field. Kurukshetra, a town in the Indian state of Haryana, is visited by pilgrims as the place where the Gita was spoken.

Other readers, Hindu and not, read the battle as an *allegory*, a story whose parts stand for something else. Gandhi wrote that the Gita's war stands for the struggle between good and evil in the human heart. Some teachers read the two armies as good and bad tendencies inside a person.

The two readings can live side by side. A reader may believe the war happened and still find the inner meaning central. A careful student describes each reading and who holds it, and does not declare one of them the correct one. Students may hold a view of their own, and still describe others' views in their holders' terms.

words.d: taking a text as describing real events as told
a story whose people and events stand for ideas or inner struggles
the field of the Mahabharata war; also a real town in Haryana, India, visited by pilgrims

look.title: Two Readers, One Verse
look.text: Reader A: "Krishna told a real prince, on a real field, to do his duty as a warrior." Reader B: "The battlefield is the mind. The cousins are my own habits. Krishna is the voice that calls me to act rightly."
look.prompt: Find one line in Gita 1 or 2 that each reader could use to support their view. Can both readings be held together?

check.q: What is an allegorical reading of the Gita's battle?
choices: The battle happened exactly as told
The battle was invented by Arnold
The battle stands for a struggle inside a person
The battle is a list of Vedic hymns
check.why: An allegory treats events as standing for ideas; Gandhi read the war as the inner struggle of good and evil.

check.q: How did Gandhi read the Gita's war?
choices: As a call to armed revolt against Britain
As a story with no moral meaning
As a history of the Mughal Empire
As the struggle between good and evil in the heart
check.why: Gandhi wrote that the war is an allegory of the inner struggle.

check.q: What should a careful student do with the two readings?
choices: Describe each and who holds it without declaring one correct
Pick the correct one and reject the other
Ignore both and read only chapter 18
Assume all Hindus hold the same reading
check.why: Academic study describes readings and their holders without taking a side.

review.q: Why does Arjuna put down his bow in Gita 1?
choices: Krishna tells him the war is over
He cannot bear to kill his kin and teachers
He wants to become a priest
review.why: Arjuna sees relatives and teachers in the other army and refuses to fight.

review.q: What image does Gita 2.22 use for rebirth?
choices: A tortoise drawing in its limbs
review.why: The clothing image is 2.22; the tortoise is 2.58; salt is in the Chandogya Upanishad; the leaf is Gita 9.26.

choices: The person of steady wisdom in Gita 2

review.q: What does Gita 2.47 teach about action?
choices: Act without being driven by the fruits
Act only when the reward is certain
review.why: Gita 2.47 says one's concern is with action, not its fruits.

review.q: Who translated the Gita into English verse as The Song Celestial?
review.why: Arnold published The Song Celestial in 1885; Telang's prose Gita appeared in 1882.

review.q: In the chain of Gita 2.62–2.63, what comes from anger?
review.why: The chain runs attachment, desire, anger, confusion, loss of memory and understanding, ruin.

review.q: Which reader holds a literal reading of Kurukshetra?
choices: One who reads the armies as good and bad habits
One who thinks the Gita was written in English
One who reads the Gita as a cookbook
One who takes the war and teaching as real events
review.why: A literal reading takes the events as told; an allegorical one reads them as inner struggle.

review.q: What does Arjuna ask of Krishna in Gita 2.7?
choices: To teach him as a disciple
To show him the salt in water
review.why: In 2.7 Arjuna asks Krishna to teach him, turning friend into guru.

chapters.title: Action Without Clinging
chapters.bigQuestion: Can a person do their work fully while letting go of what they will get from it?

story.title: The Night Train
story.kicker: After a double shift, a nurse opens a small paperback to chapter 3.
paragraphs: It is almost midnight on a Metra train heading west out of Chicago. Priya, a nurse, has just finished a sixteen-hour double shift. Her feet hurt. One of her patients did not make it through the evening, though the whole team did everything they could.

In her bag is a worn paperback Gita that her grandmother gave her. She opens it to chapter 3, a habit she has kept since nursing school. Tonight her eyes land on a line about no one being able to stay without action, even for a moment.

She thinks about the families she spoke to today. She did her work well, and still the outcome was not what anyone hoped. The Gita, as she reads it, tells her to give full care to the work and to let go of the results she cannot control.

Priya is a made-up person, but readers like her are real. Many Hindus, and many people of other backgrounds, have turned to Gita 3 to 6 while thinking about work, duty and burnout. Others argue with these chapters and ask whether "doing your duty" can go too far.

In this chapter you will read Krishna's teaching on action, knowledge and meditation, see how Gandhi read it, and practice arguing with a text respectfully. You will also ask where the idea of duty needs limits, and how Hindu readers have answered.
story.think: What part of a job is in a worker's control, and what part is not? How might that difference change how a person feels after a hard day?

lessons.title: Why Not Just Withdraw?
lessons.mainIdea: In Gita 3 Arjuna asks why he must act at all, and Krishna answers that no one can stay without action.
reading: Chapter 3 opens with a fair question. In 3.1 and 3.2 Arjuna says: if knowledge is better than action, why are you urging me into this terrible deed? Your words confuse me. Tell me one thing clearly. Arjuna is not being rude. He is asking a real student's question, and Krishna takes it seriously.

Krishna's answer in 3.4 and 3.5 is that a person does not become free from action by simply not starting it, nor reach perfection just by giving things up. No one can remain even for a moment without acting. The body breathes, eats and moves; nature itself pushes a person to act.

So the question is not whether to act, but how. The Gita's answer is *karma yoga*, the discipline of action. Verse 3.8 says to do one's assigned work, because action is better than inaction; without action, even the body could not be kept going. Karma yoga does not ask a person to stop working. It asks a person to change how they hold their work.

words.d: the discipline or path of action done without clinging to its results
giving up; in the Gita, giving up attachment rather than giving up all action
not acting; Gita 3.8 says action is better than inaction

look.title: Not for a Moment
look.text: No one ever remains even for a moment without performing some action; for everyone, being without free will in the matter, is made to act by the qualities born of nature.
look.cite: Bhagavad Gita 3.5, paraphrased from K.T. Telang's translation (SBE 8, 1882)
look.prompt: List three actions you do without choosing them. How does this verse change the question "Should I act?"

check.q: What does Arjuna ask at the start of Gita 3?
choices: Why must I act if knowledge is better?
How many verses are in the Gita?
check.why: In 3.1–3.2 Arjuna asks why he is urged to act if knowledge is superior.

check.q: What does Gita 3.5 say about action?
choices: No one can remain even a moment without acting
check.why: Verse 3.5 says nature makes everyone act.

check.q: What is karma yoga?
choices: The discipline of action without clinging to results
The study of the Rig Veda
check.why: Karma yoga is the Gita's path of action done without attachment.

lessons.title: Work as Offering
lessons.mainIdea: Gita 3.9 and 3.19 teach acting without attachment, as an offering rather than for private gain.
reading: Gita 3.9 says that action binds a person unless it is done as *yajna*. Yajna first meant the Vedic fire sacrifice. The Gita widens it. Any work done as an offering, not only for oneself, can be yajna. This widening lets a farmer, a teacher or a nurse see ordinary labor as a kind of offering.

Verse 3.19 then gives the plain instruction: therefore, without attachment, always do the work that should be done; by working without attachment a person reaches the highest. Many readers see this as the center of karma yoga. Readers note that the verse does not say to work less. It says to work without clinging.

The Gita then points to King Janaka, a wise ruler in the Upanishads, who kept ruling while being free of attachment (3.20). Krishna adds that a person should act for *lokasangraha*, the holding-together of the world. Leaders are copied by others, so their example matters.

words.d: sacrifice or offering; first the Vedic fire rite, widened by the Gita to any work offered
"holding the world together"; acting for the welfare and good order of all
doing something fully without clinging to what one gets from it

look.title: Janaka on the Throne
look.text: Gita 3.20 names Janaka, a king remembered as a wise man who kept ruling his kingdom. Krishna says Janaka and others reached perfection through action, and that one should act with an eye to holding the world together.
look.prompt: Why might the Gita choose a king, not a hermit, as its example? What does that suggest about ordinary jobs?

check.q: How does the Gita widen the meaning of yajna?
choices: Yajna means only the Soma rite
Yajna means the reading of Arnold's translation
Any work done as an offering can be yajna
check.why: The Gita extends yajna from the fire rite to work offered without selfish aim.

check.q: What does lokasangraha mean?
choices: Holding the world together, acting for the good of all
Leaving the world to live in a forest
check.why: Gita 3.20 uses lokasangraha for acting to keep the world in good order.

check.q: Who is the example of a person who acted while free of attachment in Gita 3.20?
check.why: Janaka, a wise king, is named in Gita 3.20.

lessons.title: One's Own Duty
lessons.mainIdea: Gita 3.35 says it is better to do one's own duty imperfectly than another's duty well.
reading: Gita 3.35 is short and much debated. Krishna says one's own duty, even done imperfectly, is better than another's duty done well. Death in one's own duty is better; another's duty brings danger. The word is *svadharma*, one's own dharma. Sva means "one's own." So the word points to a duty that belongs to a particular person.

In the setting of the poem, Arjuna is a *kshatriya*, a member of the warrior class, and his svadharma is to fight a just war. Traditional readers tied svadharma closely to varna, the four social classes named in the Vedic texts. That reading linked duty to birth.

Many modern Hindus read svadharma more broadly, as the calling that fits a person's nature and gifts. Critics note that the verse was used to defend a fixed social order. Reformers answer that the Gita also says, in 4.13, that varna was made by qualities and actions. The debate is ongoing inside the tradition.

words.d: one's own dharma: the duty that belongs to a particular person
the warrior and ruler class in the Vedic four-varna scheme; Arjuna is a kshatriya
one of the four social classes named in Vedic texts: priests, warriors, merchants, laborers

look.title: Two Readings of Svadharma
look.text: Reading A: svadharma is the duty of the social class one is born into. Reading B: svadharma is the calling that fits one's own nature and gifts. Both readings cite Gita 3.35; Reading B often also cites 4.13 on qualities and actions.
look.prompt: What would each reading tell a student who wants a career different from her parents'? Describe each fairly.

check.q: What does svadharma mean?
check.why: Sva means one's own; svadharma is one's own duty.

check.q: What does Gita 3.35 say?
choices: Better another's duty done well than one's own
Better one's own duty imperfect than another's done well
check.why: Gita 3.35 prefers one's own duty, even if imperfectly done.

check.q: Which verse do many reformers cite to link varna to qualities and actions?
check.why: Gita 4.13 says varna was made by qualities and actions, a verse reformers often cite.

lessons.title: When Dharma Declines
lessons.mainIdea: In Gita 4.7 to 4.8 Krishna says he comes into the world age after age to protect dharma.
reading: In chapter 4 Krishna says something new about himself. He tells Arjuna that they have both had many births; Krishna knows them all, but Arjuna does not. Then comes one of the Gita's best-known passages. The claim that Krishna remembers past births sets up the famous verses that follow.

In 4.7 and 4.8, Krishna says that whenever dharma declines and adharma, its opposite, rises, he sends himself forth. To protect the good, to destroy wrongdoers and to establish dharma, he comes into being age after age. The phrase "age after age" translates the Sanskrit yuge yuge.

Vaishnava Hindus, who worship Vishnu, read these verses as the Gita's statement of the *avatar* teaching: Vishnu descends in forms such as Rama and Krishna. The Gita itself does not list the avatars; the lists come from the Puranas. As students, we describe what the Gita says and how devotees read it.

words.d: a "descent"; a form in which Vishnu is believed by his devotees to come into the world
the opposite of dharma: disorder, injustice, wrongdoing
a Hindu who worships Vishnu or his forms, such as Krishna and Rama, as supreme

look.title: Age After Age
look.text: Whenever there is a decline of dharma and a rise of adharma, then I create myself. To protect the good, to destroy evildoers, and to establish dharma, I am born age after age.
look.cite: Bhagavad Gita 4.7–4.8, paraphrased from K.T. Telang's translation (SBE 8, 1882)
look.prompt: Who is speaking, and to whom? What three purposes does the speaker name?

check.q: According to Gita 4.7–4.8, when does Krishna say he comes into being?
choices: When dharma declines and adharma rises
check.why: The verses link Krishna's coming to the decline of dharma.

check.q: Where do the lists of Vishnu's avatars mainly come from?
check.why: The Gita states the principle; Puranas such as the Bhagavata give lists.

check.q: Which statement is written in the right academic voice?
choices: Vishnu never came into the world
We know the avatar teaching is true
Vaishnava Hindus read Gita 4.7–4.8 as teaching Vishnu's avatars
check.why: Academic study attributes the belief to Vaishnava readers without affirming or denying it.

lessons.title: Action in Inaction
lessons.mainIdea: Gita 4.18 says the wise see inaction in action and action in inaction.
reading: Gita 4.18 reads like a riddle. The one who sees inaction in action and action in inaction is wise among people and is a true yogi, even while doing all kinds of work. What can it mean? The verse sounds like a puzzle on purpose. It asks the reader to slow down and think.

Commentators give different answers. One common reading: a person acting without attachment is, inwardly, not bound by the action, so there is a kind of stillness inside the work. And a person who sits idle while wanting results is still bound, so there is hidden action in the inaction.

This is a good place to practice *close reading*. Look at each word. Ask who is being described, and what the verse is contrasting. Then compare what commentators say. The same line can bear more than one careful reading. Commentators such as Shankara and Ramanuja read many verses in different ways, as you will see in a later unit.

words.d: slow, careful reading of a passage word by word, asking what each part does
a statement that seems to contradict itself but may point to a deeper idea
a scholar who writes an explanation of a sacred text

look.title: The Riddle Verse
look.text: Gita 4.18 (paraphrase): The one who sees inaction in action, and action in inaction, is wise among people; that one is a yogi who does all work.
look.prompt: Describe a person who is busy on the outside but calm inside, and a person who is still on the outside but restless inside. Which fits each half of the verse?

check.q: What kind of statement is Gita 4.18?
choices: A paradox that seems to contradict itself
A rule for the dice game
check.why: Seeing action in inaction and inaction in action is a paradox.

check.q: On one common reading, why is a person acting without attachment said to have inaction in action?
choices: They do not really do anything
They are inwardly not bound by the work
They let others do the work
check.why: Commentators often explain that non-attachment gives inner stillness within work.

check.q: What is the first step of close reading?
choices: Look at each word and ask what it does
check.why: Close reading starts with the words of the passage itself.

lessons.title: The Fire of Knowledge
lessons.mainIdea: Gita 4 praises knowledge, jnana, as a fire that burns away the binding effects of action.
reading: Later in chapter 4 the Gita turns to knowledge, or *jnana*. Verse 4.37 says that as a blazing fire reduces fuel to ashes, so the fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes. Readers take this to mean that knowledge frees a person from the binding results of karma.

Verse 4.34 says how to gain this knowledge: by humble respect, by questions, and by service to teachers who have seen the truth. The Gita pictures learning as a relationship. That is what Arjuna himself is doing with Krishna. Knowledge in the Gita is not only facts. It is understanding passed from teacher to student.

So far the Gita has praised action and knowledge. Some readers see a tension: which is better? Krishna answers in chapter 5 that both lead to the same goal, but that the discipline of action is easier for most people. The Gita tends to join paths rather than choose only one.

words.d: knowledge, especially spiritual knowledge of the self
the path of knowledge, one of the paths the Gita describes
a student who learns from a teacher by respect, questions and service

look.title: Fire and Fuel
look.text: Gita 4.37 (paraphrase): as a blazing fire turns fuel to ashes, so the fire of knowledge turns all actions to ashes.
look.prompt: What is the fuel, and what is the fire, in this image? Why might the poet choose fire rather than water?

check.q: What does jnana mean?
check.why: Jnana is knowledge; karma is action; bhakti is devotion; yajna is sacrifice.

check.q: In Gita 4.37, what does the fire of knowledge do?
check.why: Knowledge is pictured as fire that burns the binding power of actions.

check.q: According to Gita 4.34, how does a person gain knowledge?
choices: By humble respect, questions and service to teachers
check.why: Verse 4.34 names respect, questioning and service.

lessons.title: A Seat, Neither High nor Low
lessons.mainIdea: Gita 6 describes how a person of the text sets up for meditation and steadies the mind.
reading: Chapter 6 is often called the chapter of meditation, *dhyana*. In verses 6.10 to 6.14 Krishna describes how a yogi prepares. The yogi goes to a clean place, sets a firm seat neither too high nor too low, and covers it with grass, a deer skin and a cloth.

The yogi holds body, head and neck straight and still, and gazes at the tip of the nose without looking around. The mind is to be calm and fearless. These details show that the Gita treats meditation as a practice with a body and a setting, not only an idea.

In this course we describe what the text says about meditation. We do not practice it in class. Students can notice how carefully the text builds its scene, from the seat to the gaze to the mind. Notice also what the text leaves out: it does not name a set time or a count of breaths here.

words.d: meditation: steady, focused attention described in Gita 6
a person who practices yoga, the discipline the Gita describes
the position of the body; Gita 6.13 describes a straight, still posture

look.title: Building the Scene
look.text: Gita 6.11–6.13 (summary): a clean place; a firm seat, not too high or low; grass, deer skin and cloth; body, head and neck straight; gaze steady at the tip of the nose.
look.prompt: Why do you think the text gives such specific physical details? What does it suggest about how body and mind are related in the Gita?

check.q: What is dhyana?
check.why: Dhyana is meditation, the subject of Gita 6.

check.q: What seat does Gita 6.11 describe?
choices: A throne high above the ground
A bench in a crowded hall
A firm seat neither too high nor too low
check.why: The Gita describes a firm seat, neither too high nor too low, in a clean place.

check.q: How does this course treat meditation?
choices: It describes what the text says without leading practice
check.why: In a public school we study what texts describe; we do not lead religious practice.

lessons.title: The Lamp and the Restless Mind
lessons.mainIdea: Gita 6.19 pictures the steady mind as a lamp in a windless place, and 6.34–6.35 admit the mind is hard to hold.
reading: Verse 6.19 gives a lovely image. The mind of a yogi who has mastered it is like a lamp in a windless place that does not flicker. The flame stands still, because nothing blows it about. Readers remember the picture because anyone who has watched a candle knows how easily a flame moves.

Arjuna does not simply accept this. In 6.34 he says the mind is restless, turbulent, strong and stubborn; holding it seems as hard as holding the wind. It is one of the most honest moments in the book. A student is allowed to say, "This is hard." He does not pretend to be calm when he is not.

Krishna agrees. In 6.35 he says the mind is indeed hard to control, but it can be held by *abhyasa*, steady practice, and *vairagya*, letting go. The Gita does not promise a quick fix. It describes slow, patient effort. Many readers find comfort in that honesty from both speakers.

words.d: steady, repeated practice
letting go of cravings; detachment
Arjuna's description of the mind in Gita 6.34, as hard to hold as the wind

look.title: Lamp and Wind
look.text: Gita 6.19: the steady mind is like a lamp in a windless place that does not flicker. Gita 6.34: Arjuna says holding the mind is as hard as holding the wind.
look.prompt: Both images use air. How does the second image answer the first? What does Krishna's reply in 6.35 add?

check.q: In Gita 6.19, what is the steady mind compared to?
choices: A lamp in a windless place
check.why: The unflickering lamp is the image of 6.19.

check.q: What does Arjuna say about the mind in Gita 6.34?
choices: It is as hard to hold as the wind
It is the same as the body
check.why: Arjuna admits the mind is restless and as hard to hold as the wind.

check.q: What two things does Krishna say help hold the mind in Gita 6.35?
check.why: Abhyasa (practice) and vairagya (letting go) are named in 6.35.

lessons.title: Gandhi's Gospel of Selfless Action
lessons.mainIdea: Gandhi read Gita 2 to 6 as a guide to selfless service and nonviolent action.
reading: Gandhi translated the Gita into Gujarati and called his version Anasaktiyoga, "the yoga of non-attachment" (published 1929 and 1930). For him the key teaching was acting without desire for the fruits. He saw this as the heart of public service. The book was widely read in the Indian freedom movement.

Gandhi read the Gita's battle as an allegory, and so he did not see it as a call to physical war. He argued that a person who truly acts without attachment could not harm others for gain. For him the Gita pointed toward *ahimsa*, not harming. Not every reader accepts this step, but it shaped Gandhi's whole public life.

Other readers disagreed. The nationalist leader Bal Gangadhar Tilak wrote a long study, Gita Rahasya (1915), reading the Gita as a call to energetic action in the world, including resistance. Both men were devout readers. Their debate shows how one text can guide very different lives.

words.d: "the yoga of non-attachment"; Gandhi's Gujarati Gita
not harming; a key value for Gandhi and in Jain, Buddhist and Hindu texts
Bal Gangadhar Tilak's 1915 study reading the Gita as a call to action

look.title: Some Modern Readers of the Gita
look.cite: Standard publication dates: Telang, SBE 8 (1882); Arnold (1885); Tilak (1915); Gandhi, Anasaktiyoga (1929–30)
look.prompt: These four works came out within about fifty years. What was happening in India during those years that might explain the interest?

check.q: What did Gandhi call his Gujarati Gita?
check.why: Gandhi's version is Anasaktiyoga; Gita Rahasya is Tilak's.

check.q: How did Tilak's reading differ from Gandhi's?
choices: Tilak said the Gita should not be read
Tilak stressed energetic action in the world, including resistance
Tilak read the Gita only as poetry with no teaching
Tilak read it as a Buddhist text
check.why: Tilak's Gita Rahasya read the Gita as a call to action; Gandhi stressed nonviolent selfless service.

check.q: What does ahimsa mean?
check.why: Ahimsa means non-harming.

lessons.title: Duty and Conscience
lessons.mainIdea: Readers argue about whether the Gita's call to duty leaves room for conscience, and the text itself stages the debate.
reading: Arjuna's refusal in chapter 1 can look like conscience: he feels killing kin is wrong. Krishna's answer calls him back to duty. So a hard question follows. Does the Gita teach that duty should override conscience? Readers have given at least three careful answers, and each rests on verses in the text.

Some readers say yes, within limits: Arjuna's war is a just war, fought after peace failed, and his grief is personal, not moral. Others say the Gita reshapes conscience rather than overriding it: Krishna asks Arjuna to act from a steady, unselfish mind, and 18.63 ends with "do as you choose." Still others, like some modern critics, remain uneasy about any text used to justify war.

Arguing with a sacred text is an old Hindu practice. Commentators disagreed sharply for centuries. When you argue, name the verse, name the reader, and give their reasons fairly. That is how a scholar enters the conversation without mocking anyone. It is also how a reader shows respect for people who hold the text sacred.

words.d: a person's inner sense of right and wrong
a war held to be fought for right reasons and by right means
an explanation of what a text means, given by a particular reader

look.title: Do as You Choose
look.text: Near the end of the Gita (18.63), after all the teaching, Krishna tells Arjuna: I have told you this wisdom; reflect on it fully, and then do as you choose.
look.prompt: How does 18.63 affect the debate about duty and conscience? Build one argument on each side using this verse.

check.q: Which verse ends Krishna's teaching with "do as you choose"?
check.why: In 18.63 Krishna tells Arjuna to reflect and then act as he chooses.

check.q: What is conscience?
choices: A person's inner sense of right and wrong
check.why: Conscience is the inner sense of right and wrong.

check.q: What makes an argument about a sacred text fair?
choices: Choosing the reading your friends like
Naming the verse and the reader and giving their reasons
check.why: Fair argument cites the passage and attributes each reading with its reasons.

review.q: What does Gita 3.5 say about action?
choices: No one can stay even a moment without acting
review.why: Verse 3.5 says nature makes everyone act.
Svadharma, one's own dharma, is the subject of Gita 3.35.

review.q: Who is speaking in Gita 4.7–4.8, the verses about coming age after age?
review.why: Krishna speaks of coming into being when dharma declines.

review.q: What image does Gita 6.19 use for a steady mind?
choices: A lamp in a windless place
review.why: 6.19 is the lamp; 2.22 clothes; 4.37 fire; 2.58 tortoise.

review.q: What does yajna mean in the Gita's widened sense?
review.why: The Gita extends yajna from fire sacrifice to offered work.

review.q: What two things does Gita 6.35 say help control the mind?
review.why: Abhyasa and vairagya are named in 6.35.

review.q: Who is King Janaka in Gita 3.20?
choices: A wise king who acted without attachment
A sage who wrote the Gita
review.why: Janaka is the Gita's example of a ruler who reached perfection through action.
